abstract: Severe neutropenia predisposes patients to life-threatening infections, while donor-dependent granulocyte transfusions are limited by availability and variable cell quality. Here, we engineered human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) to constitutively or inducibly express angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) and differentiated them into functional ACE-engineered neutrophils (ACE-iNeu). ACE expression enhanced granulocytic maturation, reactive oxygen species generation, inflammatory cytokine production, and antimicrobial signaling. ACE-iNeu exhibited enhanced bactericidal activity against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Following adoptive transfer into neutropenic mice, ACE-iNeu significantly reduced circulating and tissue bacterial burdens. Integrated metabolomic and transcriptomic analyses revealed ACE-associated alterations in adenine nucleotide abundance and developmental and inflammatory pathways. Together, these findings establish ACE engineering as a strategy to enhance the production and antimicrobial function of human iPSC-derived neutrophils and support further preclinical development of engineered granulocyte therapies for severe drug-resistant infections.
hook: Engineered stem-cell neutrophils kill drug-resistant bacteria better and cut bacterial load in mice.

summary: Human stem cells were engineered to express angiotensin-converting enzyme and turned into neutrophils that killed MRSA and multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas more effectively. Given to neutropenic mice, they lowered bacterial burdens in blood and tissue. This is early preclinical work in mice, and safety and scale-up are not addressed.
title: ACE-engineered human iPSC-derived neutrophils enhance host defense against multidrug-resistant bacterial infections
